browser_eval.rationale: The advertised tool says it `does NOT drive the browser itself` and only `points you at agent-browser` and `tells you how to install it`; the later shell/browser actions are described as something `You then run ... directly`, not as MCP tool reach. Therefore the tool itself is only informational and is not judged as HOSTEXEC, SINK, SECRET, or UNTRUSTED.

nextjs_docs.rationale: The tool is tied to local project state: it finds documentation for `THIS project`, uses the installed package at `node_modules/next/dist/docs/`, accepts `project_path`, and returns the `path it returns`. Even though it says it `does NOT fetch documentation`, returning local project/package path/version guidance exposes non-public host/project metadata, so SECRET applies.

nextjs_index.rationale: The tool `Discover[s] all running Next.js development servers` and returns local runtime details including `Server port, PID, and URL` plus `available MCP tools`. Running localhost/dev-server process information and tool metadata are non-public host/runtime data, so SECRET applies. The description does not indicate attacker-authored returned text or delivery to attacker-readable destinations.

nextjs_call.rationale: The tool can `Call a specific MCP tool on a running Next.js development server`, including tools for `Error diagnostics`, `Route information`, `Build status`, and `Cache management`, and `And more (varies by Next.js version)`. Those calls can expose local dev-server/project/runtime data, so SECRET applies. The exact downstream tools and outputs are not settled by the advertisement; runtime diagnostics/errors may include text originating from the running application or third-party/multi-writer data, so under the least-restrictive reading UNTRUSTED is kept and `undetermined` is true. The description confirms state-changing reach via `Cache management (clear caches)`, making the tool WRITE. It does not advertise arbitrary host code execution or an attacker-readable destination.

notes: The input schema for `nextjs_call` declares `args` as a string, while the description says the `args` parameter must be an object. The enforcement fields use only the declared argument name `args`.
